fields.Front: What are the 'rules of the game' for representing relationships using only tables?
fields.Back: You may add as many new columns and rows as you want to existing tables, and you may add new tables; that is all (columns, rows, tables).

fields.Front: How is a 1:N relationship mapped (PROFESSOR M --- Works for --- 1 DEPARTMENT)?
fields.Back: Put the primary key of the 1 side (DeptID) as a foreign key column in the table of the N side (PROFESSOR); e.g. Laura, Doug, Jamie -> CS; Stuart, Irving -> MA; Michael -> PS.

fields.Front: Why does the foreign key go on the N (many) side of a 1:N relationship?
fields.Back: Each N-side row relates to at most one 1-side row, so a single cell suffices; the 1 side would need a list of keys (not atomic).

fields.Front: Where do the attributes of a 1:N relationship go (e.g. Hours, StartDate on Works for)?
fields.Back: Into the N-side table along with the foreign key (PROFESSOR gets DeptID, Hours, StartDate).

fields.Text: After mapping Works for, PROFESSOR has primary key {{c1::EmpID}} and foreign key {{c2::DeptID}}; DEPARTMENT has primary key DeptID and {{c3::no foreign keys yet}}.

fields.Front: How is a 1:1 relationship mapped (PROFESSOR 1 --- Chairs --- 1 DEPARTMENT)?
fields.Back: Put the primary key of one side as a foreign key in the other's table: either ManageDeptID in PROFESSOR (many NULLs) or ManagerID in DEPARTMENT (no NULLs: 18 MA, 34 CS, 15 PS).

fields.Front: For a 1:1 relationship, which table should receive the foreign key, and why?
fields.Back: The one with total participation (DEPARTMENT for Chairs, since every department has a chair) to avoid nulls; PROFESSOR would be mostly NULL because most professors chair nothing.

fields.Front: After mapping Chairs into DEPARTMENT: PK and FKs of PROFESSOR and DEPARTMENT?
fields.Back: PROFESSOR: PK EmpID, FK DeptID. DEPARTMENT: PK DeptID, FK ManagerID.

fields.Front: Book/Publisher/MovieDeal example: map Publishes (1 Publisher : M Book) and Accepts (1 Book : 1 MovieDeal, attribute AcceptDate).
fields.Back: Book(ISBN, Title, Price, Author, Available, PubID FK); MovieDeal(Deal_ID, NegotiatorName, StudioName, HeadScreenWriter, ISBN FK, AcceptDate); Publisher(PubID, PubName, Address).

fields.Text: For a 1:N relationship the foreign key goes in the table on the {{c1::N (many)}} side; for a 1:1 relationship it goes in the table with {{c2::total participation}}.

fields.Front: How do foreign keys indicate a relationship between tuples?
fields.Back: A foreign key value in one row equals the primary key value of the related row in the other table (e.g. Laura's DeptID = CS links her to the Computer Science row).

fields.Front: What wrong idea does the instructor consider first for representing Works for, and why does it fail?
fields.Back: Adding a column to DEPARTMENT listing Laura's, Doug's and Jamie's IDs separated by commas; it fails because tables must be normalized (one value per cell), so nothing can be done in the department table.

fields.Front: Does the foreign key column added for a 1:N relationship have to have a particular name?
fields.Back: No; the instructor calls it DeptID but could have called it WorksInID. The star on the slide marks it as a foreign key.

fields.Front: Using the professor and department tables, how do you answer 'which building does Laura Reid work in?'
fields.Back: Laura's DeptID is CS; look up CS in DEPARTMENT: Middlesex College. Keys are used to answer queries across tables.

fields.Text: Hours and StartDate on Works for become columns of PROFESSOR but are {{c1::not foreign keys}}; only {{c2::DeptID}} is, because it refers back to the department table.

fields.Front: How does the instructor read the participation lines on the Chairs relationship?
fields.Back: Single line on the professor side: a professor chairs zero or one departments (partial). Double line on the department side: every department must have a chair (total).

fields.Front: For a 1:1 relationship, what if both sides have total participation? Both partial?
fields.Back: Both total: it does not matter which side gets the foreign key. Both partial: it probably does not matter, but pick the side that gives fewer nulls.

fields.Text: For a 1:1 relationship, always move the key from the {{c1::partial}} side into the {{c2::total}} side so you do not end up with a bunch of null values.

fields.Front: Book/Publisher/MovieDeal: why does ISBN go into MOVIE DEAL rather than Deal_ID into BOOK, and where does AcceptDate go?
fields.Back: MovieDeal has total participation in Accepts, so fewer nulls; AcceptDate goes with the key into MovieDeal but is not a foreign key.

fields.Front: What are the objectives of the 1:1 and 1:N mapping video?
fields.Back: Represent a relationship from an ER diagram as tables, columns and rows, and show what a foreign key is in a table.
